_note: Quenya interface, and **it is 30% of the catalogue rather than 100%, which is the finding rather than a shortfall**. The rest of the keys are absent, so they fall back to English: `data/i18n/` is a partial-overlay design by construction -- "a key it omits falls back to English rather than rendering a bare key, so a half-translated language degrades to a mixed interface instead of a broken one" -- and this is the first language that has needed that property for a reason other than being unfinished. SOURCE: every root is attested in Tolkien's Late Quenya, taken from Eldamo's `l="q"` set with no reliability mark or with `#` (derivable from an attested form by a grammatical rule). Inflected forms are regular compositions on those roots -- `lambi` the plural of `lambë`, `hentalyë` the 2nd-person polite of `henta-`, `tengwaron` the genitive plural of `tengwa` -- which Eldamo does not index because it indexes lemmas, and their absence from the index is therefore not evidence. What IS evidence is a *root* being absent, and that is what cut this catalogue in half: `hep-` (keep, for Save), `cil-` (choose, for the two Choose-a-face controls -- only the noun `cilmë` "choice" survives), `mauya-` (compel, for Essential and for "both fields are needed"), `valdë` (worth, for Priority and Importance), `munta` (nothing, for four separate empty-state strings), `nossë` (family), `nótë` (number), `palúrë` (surface, for Card width), `cirissë` (slash, for Divider), `erya` (sole), `vére` (own, for Custom), and `tengwal` -- twelve roots that a Neo-Quenya writer would supply from the reconstructed lexicon and that Tolkien did not. `holya-` "to shut" exists and is excluded too: Eldamo marks it `?`, meaning speculative, so the Close button has no verb. There is also **no attested Quenya word for column, for row, for size, for colour as an abstraction, for print, for page, or for translate**, which is most of a format panel. REGISTER: the imperative particle `á` before the verb stem, which is Tolkien's own construction (`á vala Manwë`, `á tule`, `á hyamë`) and the only imperative Quenya has. So buttons read `á napanë` "add", `á lelta` "send", `á cenë` "look at". `áva` for a negative imperative, likewise attested. TERMS: `parma` is a book or written document and stands in for the sheet; `cendelë` is a face, and using it for a printed side is the same metaphor English makes, flagged here as the one extension of sense in the catalogue. Also: `tengwa` = letter, `tengwar` = the letters, `quetta` = word, `lambë` = language, `canta` = shape or framework, for the Format panel; `nat` = thing, `nati` = the items; `lantalca` = boundary mark, which is exactly a margin; `asta` = a division or part, for a section; `raxë` = danger, for the emergency colour; `lúmë` = time; `men` = way. INTERPOLATION -- and Quenya is the sharpest case in the whole project. A placeholder is a plain string substitution, and **Quenya's ten cases are all suffixal and all have allomorphs chosen by the stem's final sound**: the instrumental is `-nen` after a vowel and `-inen` after a consonant, the allative `-nna` assimilates to `-nda` after `-n`, the plural is `-r` after a vowel and `-i` otherwise. So a template may never put a case suffix after a placeholder, and the first draft of this file did it five times: `{language}nen`, `{regions}ssë`, `{faces}llo`, `{total}llo`. Every one is now a bare noun beside a dash or an adjacent head word -- `i nassë — {language}`, `{language} parma` -- so the grammar hangs off Quenya's own word and the insert stays inert. That is the same repair the Hungarian and Indonesian catalogues record, and Quenya needs it more than either, because Hungarian's `-ban/-ben` at least fails audibly where Quenya's would produce a form that looks like a different case. The article is the second trap and it is avoided the same way: `i` is invariable, so it is safe before a placeholder, but the adjective agreement is not -- a plural adjective takes `-ë` or `-i` depending on its own shape, so no template here puts an adjective in agreement with an inserted noun. Serif and Sans and the romanisation-system names stay Latin, as in the Greek and Indonesian catalogues.
